To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the position of the $0-\pi $ impurity quantum phase boundary in the weakly correlated regime is given by $V_g=\Delta$ and in the strongly correlated (Kondo) regime is given by $(\pi/2-\phi_0) = \arcsin\left(\frac{\Delta}{\Gamma}\right)$, where $V_g$ is the gate voltage, $\Delta$ the superconducting gap, $\phi_0$ the superconductivity phase difference

the position of the $0-\pi\,$ transition in the parameter space of the single-impurity Anderson model is given by the following two simple analytical formula: $\mu_c = \frac{U}{2} - \Delta$ for weakly correlated systems, and $T_K = 2\Delta$ for strongly correlated systems.

(i) the $0-\pi $ impurity quantum phase transitions in the weakly correlated regime are described by a single analytical formula, (ii) the Kondo regime is described by a second formula, and (iii) the two-level approximation can be used to determine the phase boundary from measured data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physics of quantum phase transitions in quantum-dot-based Josephson junctions.
the physics of a single quantum dot coupled to superconducting leads, which is one of the most fundamental models for the description of superconductor/quantum dot hybrid systems.
the interplay of quantum phase transitions and superconducting correlations in quantum-dot-based Josephson junctions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a superconducting quantum dot with an even number of electrons is a promising candidate for a quantum phase transition in the experimentally accessible regime of parameters.

the quantum phase transition can be observed experimentally in the superconducting quantum dot, which makes it a promising candidate for the experimental realization of the Kosterlitz-Thouless quantum phase transition.
the $0-\pi $ impurity quantum phase transitions in quantum dot based Josephson junctions are well understood and can be reliably predicted and measured in experiments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a superconducting quantum dot is a very good candidate for the realization of the quantum phase transition in a solid state system.

the quantum phase transition in the superconducting quantum dot can be experimentally detected by measuring the current-voltage characteristics in a wide range of temperatures, and that the transition can be tuned by the gate voltage and the phase difference.
the $0-\pi $ quantum phase transition can be observed in quantum dot-based tunable Josephson junctions at temperatures as high as 10-15 K.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a quantum phase transition in a quantum dot-based Josephson junction can be observed at finite temperatures.
quantum phase transitions in quantum dot systems are not a mere theoretical curiosity but can be studied in real experiments with the help of the newly developed analytical and numerical tools.
the phase boundary is not a sharp line in the parameter space of a quantum dot, but rather an extended phase region.
